summary: The paper studies Mamba's in-context learning capabilities on random Markov chains, showing empirically that a single-layer Mamba learns the optimal Laplacian smoothing estimator, and proving theoretically (for a simplified variant, MambaZero, and first-order chains only) that such a representation exists. The central ablation identifying convolution as the key mechanism is compelling and the constructive proof is a genuine theoretical contribution. However, a material gap exists between the theoretical scope (k=1, L1-normalised MambaZero) and the broader claims throughout the paper (all Markov orders, full Mamba), the statistical evidence is thin (5 seeds, no significance tests, Table 1 lacks error bars), and the natural-language experiments are too limited to carry the generality claims in Section 5.
strengths: Theorem 1 provides a constructive, mechanistically interpretable proof that MambaZero can exactly represent the Laplacian estimator for first-order Markov chains; the construction aligns with empirically observed parameter patterns (at≈1, b(ij)·ct≈0), making it one of the more satisfying theory-meets-experiment arguments in SSM expressivity work.

The ablation isolating convolution (Fig. 3a, MambaZero vs. full Mamba vs. Mamba-without-conv) is clean and decisive; the observation that the convolution window must be at least k+1 (Fig. 3b) is a crisp, falsifiable and empirically verified prediction.
Theorem 2 (information-theoretic lower bound on recurrent hidden dimension) is a principled complement to the upper bound in Theorem 1, and the proof generalises to arbitrary recurrent depth.
The switching-Markov extension (Sec. 5.1) is a well-designed probe of the selectivity mechanism and provides interpretable evidence that at tracks switch events.
The paper is honest that the main focus is representation power, not a Mamba-vs-Transformer competition, and this framing keeps the narrative coherent.

key_concerns.issue: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion repeatedly claim Mamba learns the optimal estimator 'for all Markov orders,' but Theorem 1 is only proved for k=1. For k>1 the paper provides only empirical evidence (Fig. 1b). The Theorem's title ('represents the Laplacian estimator') and the paper's title ('From Markov to Laplace') invite a reading that is strictly stronger than what is theoretically established.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either extend Theorem 1 to general k (likely feasible given the window-size argument in Sec. 4.2.1 and the proof sketch), or prominently downgrade all multi-order claims to 'empirically suggested but not theoretically established,' including rewriting the abstract. At minimum, add a theorem/proposition for k>1 lower bounding or characterising when the construction works.

key_concerns.issue: The theoretical results are proved for MambaZero, which replaces softmax with L1-normalisation and removes ReLU/gating. The connection between MambaZero's representational result and the full Mamba architecture (which does use softmax) is asserted but never formally bridged. L1 normalisation and softmax have different fixed-point structures and the approximation gap is not quantified.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either prove a formal approximation lemma (MambaZero with L1 norm ε-approximates Mamba with softmax), or show empirically that the trained full Mamba's internal activations satisfy the same structural conditions (at≈1, b(ij)·ct≈0 with softmax) and that the KL gap attributable to the normalisation difference is negligible.

key_concerns.issue: Statistical evidence is consistently thin. Variance in Figs. 1 and 3 is reported over only 5 seeds, with no significance tests. Table 1 (WikiText-103) reports single point estimates with no error bars at all, making it impossible to assess whether the 11% perplexity improvement for Mamba is statistically meaningful or within run-to-run variance.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report at least 3-5 seeds for all experiments including Table 1; add confidence intervals or standard deviations; for Table 1, run each configuration at least three times. A paired test or bootstrap interval would strengthen the natural-language claim.

key_concerns.issue: The natural-language section (Sec. 5.2) is too thin to support the generalisation claim. One dataset (WikiText-103), one model scale (~14.5 M params), no held-out test set perplexities reported (only validation?), and no comparison to larger or deeper models beyond a qualitative remark about relative importance decreasing with depth (Tables 4-5 in appendix).
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Test on at least one additional dataset (e.g. Penn Treebank or a larger OpenWebText split); include a second model scale; report test-set perplexity; move key ablations from the appendix into the main text if the claim about convolution on natural language is to be a first-class contribution.

key_concerns.issue: Theorem 2 states a lower bound on hidden dimension for 'a recurrent model of the form Ht = ht(Ht-1, xt).' The corollary that Mamba 'requires hidden dimension exponential in k' treats this general lower bound as applying specifically to Mamba, but Mamba's selective state-update may fall outside or at the boundary of the general recurrence form assumed. The contrast with transformers ('linear in k with three layers') cites Rajaraman et al. 2024 but does not check whether that result is directly comparable (same task, same error notion).
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Verify explicitly that Mamba's recurrence satisfies the conditions of Theorem 2, or state clearly it is a conjecture. When making the transformer comparison, align the error metric (ℓ∞ vs. L1 vs. KL) and note differences in assumptions.

key_concerns.issue: The Limitations section (p. 12) is boilerplate and does not specifically identify the k=1 restriction of Theorem 1, the L1/softmax discrepancy, or the limited scale of experiments as concrete scope boundaries.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Replace the generic limitations with the three concrete ones above; this will also help calibrate the reader's expectations more honestly.

key_concerns.issue: Several references in the text are anonymised as '[Author] et al., 2024/2025,' including references that appear to be the authors' own concurrent work on transformers and induction heads. This makes it impossible to assess whether the Markov-ICL framework is being properly credited and whether the comparison to transformer results is self-consistent.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: No action needed from authors during review (this is a double-blind artefact), but reviewers should be aware this limits the ability to verify related-work completeness.

questions_for_authors: Can Theorem 1 be extended to k>1 using the window-size argument sketched in Sec. 4.2.1? If so, what is the required hidden dimension as a function of k and S, and does it match or exceed the lower bound in Theorem 2?

The proof uses L1 normalisation instead of softmax. Is there a formal quantitative bound on how much the KL divergence increases when the L1 normalisation is replaced by softmax at the same parameter values?

For Figure 1b (L1 distance vs. Markov order), how does single-layer Mamba perform relative to the theoretical lower bound on hidden dimension from Theorem 2 as k increases? Does the model start to degrade at the predicted threshold?

In Table 1, are the perplexity numbers on validation or test? Were the hyperparameters (learning rate, warm-up, etc.) tuned separately for each ablation configuration, or held fixed? If held fixed, is there a risk that the baseline (without conv) is under-tuned?

The switching-Markov experiment (Sec. 5.1) is qualitative. Can you quantify how closely at tracks switch events, e.g., via the receiver-operating-characteristic curve of using at<threshold as a switch detector?
MambaZero sets at=1 by forcing a or delta to zero. Does the full Mamba model also reach at≈1 at convergence in all experiments, including those on WikiText-103? If not, does the theory still apply?
calibration_check: The title and abstract claim that single-layer Mamba learns the optimal Laplacian estimator 'for all Markov orders,' but the main theorem (Theorem 1) is proved only for k=1 on a simplified architecture with L1 normalisation; the multi-order and natural-language generalisations are empirically suggested but not formally established, creating a systematic overclaim relative to the evidence.

significance.justification: Connecting Mamba to the Laplacian smoothing estimator and identifying convolution as the key mechanism is a useful insight for the SSM community, but the theoretical scope is narrow (k=1, MambaZero) and the natural-language evidence is too thin for the result to immediately change practice.

novelty.justification: To the best of this reviewer's assessment, this is the first constructive representational proof linking Mamba to an optimal Bayesian estimator and the first use of the Markov-ICL framework for SSMs, both of which are genuinely new contributions.

rigor.justification: Theorem 1 is constructive and its proof sketch is mechanistically grounded, but the L1/softmax discrepancy and the k=1 restriction create a meaningful gap between the proved result and the claimed scope; Theorem 2's applicability to full Mamba is asserted without verification.

statistical_soundness.justification: Five seeds with standard deviation is barely adequate for the Markov experiments; Table 1 reports single-run perplexities with no variance estimate; no significance tests are applied anywhere despite quantitative comparative claims.

calibration_honesty.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion repeatedly assert that Mamba learns the optimal estimator 'for all Markov orders,' which is empirically supported but theoretically only proved for k=1; the Limitations section does not identify this gap.

clarity.justification: The paper is well-organised and the key mechanism is explained with good intuition in Sec. 4.2.1; the notation is standard and the proof sketch is readable, though the plain-text extraction garbles some equations.

structure_compliance.justification: The paper follows a standard Abstract/Introduction/Related Work/Setup/Theory/Experiments/Conclusion structure appropriate for ICLR; the main text is approximately 12 pages with detailed appendices.

reproducibility.justification: Experimental details are deferred to appendix F (not visible), hyperparameters for Table 1 are not stated in the main text, and model architecture parameters (N, d, e) for the trained models are not tabulated; the theoretical construction in Sec. 4.2 is explicit enough to reproduce in principle.

related_work.justification: The coverage of SSM expressivity and ICL literature appears adequate for the claims made, but several key comparator references are anonymised, and the comparison to transformer complexity results (Rajaraman et al. 2024) is not carefully aligned in terms of error metrics.

figure_quality.justification: From the captions, Figures 1 and 3 appear well-designed and directly address the core claims; Figure 2 is an architecture diagram that aids understanding; Table 1 is informative but lacks error bars, limiting its evidentiary weight.

breadth_generality.justification: The theory covers only first-order Markov chains and a simplified architecture; the natural-language results span one dataset at one scale; the baseline set is minimal (two transformer depths, one ablation variant), making the generality claims significantly under-supported.

overall_recommendation.justification: The paper has a real theoretical contribution and a clean empirical story, but the systematic mismatch between the theoretical scope (k=1, MambaZero, L1 norm) and the paper's stated contribution (all Markov orders, full Mamba), combined with thin statistical evidence and limited natural-language experiments, pushes this below the ICLR acceptance bar in its current form.
